claims.text: Spark plasma sintering can be used to produce Mg-containing multi-principal-element alloys.
Rapidly processed Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys initially contain a supersaturated, metastable matrix that retains Mg in solid solution.
The initial SPS-processed alloy contains minimal intermetallic precipitates.
SPS can retain a homogeneous solid-solution structure without phase segregation.
Annealing or prolonged environmental exposure drives Mg partitioning out of solid solution.
Mg partitioning causes nucleation and growth of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds.
The Mg-rich intermetallic compounds form preferentially at grain boundaries and also within the matrix.
Mg-containing SPS alloys can contain Mg-rich and other intermetallic phases.
TiO2-rich surface films can enhance passivation and lower corrosion current density in an Mg-containing multi-principal-element alloy.
Discrete Mg-rich intermetallics perturb the continuity and composition of protective Al- or Ti-based oxide films.
Removal of Mg from solid solution reduces any strengthening contribution from dissolved Mg.
Intermetallic precipitation makes the oxide scale less protective and accelerates corrosion.
The annealed or aged alloy will have a statistically significant increase in corrosion current density relative to the as-sintered control.
The annealed or aged alloy will show reduced high-temperature oxidation resistance, such as greater weight gain or a discontinuous oxide scale.
Potentiodynamic polarization in 0.1 M NaCl can compare corrosion behavior of Mg-containing multi-principal-element alloys.
Oxidation near 700 degrees Celsius in an oxygen-rich atmosphere will permit observation of the proposed diffusion-driven evolution and oxide-scale degradation.
The hypothesis is restricted to non-equilibrium alloys with density below 6 g/cm3.
The kinetics of Mg partitioning and intermetallic nucleation depend on composition and processing history.
